nature-nbs-195.title: Beaver dams: flood control built by rodents
nature-nbs-195.text: The largest known beaver dam is 775 metres long. Most run from a few metres to about 100 metres. A beaver dam creates a pond that protects its builders from predators and stores food for winter. By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a {{ref:nature-eco-301}} and as an {{ref:nature-es-086}}. In their native range, the dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks. A dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and keeping streams flowing in dry spells. Bacteria in the debris behind it turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some pesticides. In Alberta, beaver ponds held 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams. Dams can also flood farmland, roads and railways. In Tierra del Fuego, introduced beavers are considered a plague. When dams are abandoned, their wetlands become meadows and then forest, slowly building up the valley floor.

nature-nbs-179.title: Flood peak attenuation: flattening the spike
nature-nbs-179.text: Flood water tends to rise and fall very abruptly. Flood peak attenuation means slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered. Many natural features do this. Marshes, river meanders, vegetation and porous materials each slow part of the flow. So does a river spreading out over its floodplain. Together they blunt the spike, so less water arrives at any one moment.

nature-nbs-182.title: Flood risk mapping: knowing where the water will go
nature-nbs-182.text: In Bangladesh, nearly 80% of people live on low floodplains. Hazard maps there pick out the areas prone to repeated or severe floods. Flood risk mapping means drawing maps of where floods may reach, so policy makers can make informed decisions. It is described as the most effective way to reduce risk to people and property, and most countries have such maps. Flood modeling adds detail. It simulates flood hazards, how their drivers interact, and their effects on people and the environment.

nature-nbs-180.title: Managed retreat from floodplains: giving land back to the river
nature-nbs-180.text: Sometimes the best flood defense is to leave. Managed retreat from floodplains means removing buildings from flood-prone areas and turning the land into parks or wilderness. Nothing is left to damage, and the floodplain is free to flood. Programs in which governments buy out floodplain homeowners ({{ref:nature-nbs-042}}) have run in New Jersey, in Charlotte in North Carolina, and in Missouri.

nature-nbs-181.title: Storm surge barriers: gates against the sea
nature-nbs-181.text: The North Sea flood of 1953 led to a new kind of defense. A storm surge barrier is a floodgate built to stop a storm surge or spring tide from flooding the area behind it. London's Thames Barrier has operated since 1982 to guard against surges like that of 1953. A barrier is almost always part of a larger system of floodwalls, levees and natural features. Storm surge warnings help decide when to close the gates.

nature-nbs-169.title: Barriers to green infrastructure: the funding gap
nature-nbs-169.text: Above all, green infrastructure is held back by a lack of funding. There is a silver lining. Because green projects produce many benefits, they can compete for many different funding sources at once. Some government tax incentive programs can also attract finance. Fragile states face harder limits. Weak governance and limited institutional capacity can stop them benefiting from green infrastructure investment.

nature-nbs-162.title: Blue infrastructure: the water in the city
nature-nbs-162.text: Rivers, ponds, lakes and harbours are infrastructure too. Blue infrastructure is the part of a city's infrastructure that involves water. Combined with green infrastructure, it becomes blue-green infrastructure. It can support aquatic insects, amphibians and water birds in the middle of a city. When people can reach it, blue infrastructure is called blue space, and access to it may benefit their health and wellbeing.

nature-nbs-164.title: Floating wetlands: gardens that clean the water beneath
nature-nbs-164.text: A wetland can float. A constructed floating wetland is a planted structure that rides on a lake, river, estuary or coastal water and supports wetland vegetation. Its plants dangle roots into the water and can remove heavy metals and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. They may store carbon too. The rafts give habitat to insects and wildlife and soften the look of hardened urban shorelines.

nature-nbs-165.title: Downspout disconnection: unplugging the roof from the sewer
nature-nbs-165.text: In heavy rain, a building's downspouts can pour 12 gallons of water a minute into the sewer. That raises the risk of basement backups and sewer overflows. Downspout disconnection cuts a roof's downspout off from the sewer and sends the roof water onto ground that can soak it up. It is especially useful in cities with combined sewer systems, where rainwater and sewage share the same pipes.

nature-nbs-163.title: Green and blue roofs: putting the roof to work
nature-nbs-163.text: Since 1991, Zurich has required that flat roofs not used as terraces be greened. Roofs can be covered with plants and soil, as in a {{ref:nature-nbs-001}}, or built to collect and hold rainfall, as in a {{ref:nature-nbs-025}}. A planted roof can hold back forty to eighty percent of the rain that falls on it and release the rest slowly. It also improves air and water quality and lowers energy costs. A water-holding roof stores rainfall and drains it to sewers and waterways at a controlled rate.

nature-nbs-170.title: Green infrastructure planning: mapping nature's work first
nature-nbs-170.text: Green infrastructure planning starts by mapping what the natural environment does for a place. It then protects the key natural areas through regulation or planning policy. Where natural life-support functions are missing, plans may add them through landscaping or engineering. In the UK the approach now appears in national, regional and local planning documents. In the US, programs run by the EPA aim to improve water quality by managing stormwater runoff more widely and easing the load on sewers.

nature-nbs-166.title: Stormwater basins: hollows that catch the rain
nature-nbs-166.text: A stormwater basin is a planted hollow in the ground that collects rainwater. It cuts runoff to sewers, reduces erosion, filters water and prevents flooding. Older basins were mowed grass. Newer designs use sturdier plants and are often called bioretention basins. They are good at removing pollutants and trapping sediment. Stormwater basins are an important part of the sponge city idea for managing floods.

nature-nbs-187.title: Floodplain restoration: reconnecting rivers to their land
nature-nbs-187.text: At Nijmegen, engineers moved a dike 350 metres inland and dug a side channel. Peak water levels fell by about 35 cm. That is floodplain restoration: returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its state before levees were built and wetlands drained. It is a nature-based solution that lowers flood risk by helping the ecosystem slow and hold water. Methods reconnect rivers to floodplains by setting back levees, removing dams or weirs, and restoring drained wetlands. The goals include fewer floods, habitat for aquatic species, cleaner water and more groundwater recharge. Vegetation helps: it can cut wave energy during floods by about 70% in salt marshes and 65% in mangroves. Restoration works best for frequent, low to moderate floods and helps little against extreme floods on its own. Coastal wetlands are accepted as large carbon sinks, but whether restoration raises their storage rates is debated. Projects can stall when immediate flood defense and current land uses are valued above ecological benefits.

nature-nbs-188.title: Stream restoration: healing rivers for fish, floods and people
nature-nbs-188.text: A US database built in the 2000s held over 35,000 stream restoration projects. Stream restoration is work to improve a river or stream's environmental health, for biodiversity, recreation, flood control or landscape. It differs from river engineering, which alters water bodies for navigation, flood control or water supply without an ecological aim. Activities range from fixing a culvert or removing a weir that blocks fish, to stabilizing banks, restoring riparian zones or adding constructed wetlands. Projects usually begin by assessing climate, geology, hydrology, sediment movement, channel shape and flood records. Approaches split in two. Form-based restoration physically reshapes the stream; process-based restoration revives its natural water and sediment processes. How well any of it works remains poorly measured, because data are thin, monitoring is scarce and yardsticks differ. Even so, it is entering law, as in the European water framework's commitment to restore surface waters.

nature-nbs-199.title: Dam removal: letting rivers run free again
nature-nbs-199.text: About 900 US dams were removed between 1990 and 2015, and by 2015 the pace was 50 to 60 a year. Dam removal means demolishing a dam to return natural flow to a river. The decision weighs a dam's benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against its harms. Dams can reduce a river's biological productivity, its biodiversity and its native species. As they age, they weaken, fill with sediment and cost more to maintain. Many removals aim to restore river habitat and native fish, as in the Elwha Ecosystem Restoration. Released sediment can rebuild habitat downstream, but toxic sediment can do harm, as when PCBs escaped after a Hudson River dam came down. Removal is always costly, and owners and government usually share the bill. Europe counts at least 150 000 barriers in its rivers that no longer serve a purpose. The EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to restore free flow to 25,000 kilometres of river by 2030.

nature-nbs-214.title: What urban floods cost
nature-nbs-214.text: FEMA says almost 40% of small businesses never reopen after a flooding disaster. Urban floods impose financial costs on property owners, businesses and cities. US experts estimate that wet basements can lower property values by 10%-25%. Urban flooding is estimated to cost £270 million a year in England and Wales. Warming would raise the bill. Under 2–4°C of warming, expected annual surface water damages in the UK may rise by £60–200 million.

nature-nbs-213.title: Grey infrastructure: fighting water with concrete
nature-nbs-213.text: Grey infrastructure is conventional infrastructure such as dams, sea walls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water. Its logic is to centralize water in big reservoirs, speed it through pipes and fight it with higher walls. That is the opposite of sponge city design. It can prevent flood damage and be economically valuable. But models suggest it may grow less effective as climate change intensifies floods. Overused, it can cause water shortages, pollution and the loss of water ecosystem services.

nature-nbs-215.title: Integrated urban water management: one city, one water
nature-nbs-215.text: Integrated urban water management handles a city's freshwater, wastewater and stormwater together, as parts of one plan for the river basin. It is seen as a way to achieve the goals of water-sensitive urban design. Treating the urban water cycle as a whole aims to use resources more efficiently, with economic, social and environmental gains. Integrated stormwater management, for example, can improve runoff quality, cut flood risk and add to the drinking water supply.

nature-nbs-212.title: Three kinds of urban flood
nature-nbs-212.text: Planners distinguish three kinds of urban flood. Pluvial floods come from heavy rain. Fluvial floods come from a river overflowing. Coastal floods often come from storm surges. Each type has different impacts and needs different defenses. Erratic rainfall is expected to make both pluvial and fluvial flooding more frequent and severe. Coastal cities may be hit hardest, facing rising seas and heavier rain at once.

nature-nbs-159.title: Subsurface flow wetlands: cleaning water out of sight
nature-nbs-159.text: In a subsurface flow constructed wetland, wastewater flows among plant roots below a gravel surface, so no water shows on top. Keeping the water hidden makes the system more efficient and less smelly. It also attracts fewer mosquitoes and suffers less in winter. It needs less land than a surface flow wetland. Its cost depends mainly on the sand used to fill the bed. It is a secondary treatment, so solids must first be removed in a primary treatment step.

nature-nbs-160.title: Surface flow wetlands: open water that kills germs
nature-nbs-160.text: A surface flow constructed wetland, also called a free water surface wetland, has open water flowing horizontally across plant roots. It is used to polish the effluent from wastewater treatment plants and to treat stormwater drainage. In the open water, sunlight, predators, settling and natural decay destroy pathogens. The drawbacks are real. It needs more land than a subsurface system, may smell more and works less well in winter. Open water can also breed mosquitoes, which makes it harder to fit into city neighborhoods.

nature-nbs-185.title: Infiltration trenches: gravel that lets rain sink in
nature-nbs-185.text: An infiltration trench is a shallow trench filled with gravel or rock. It holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater. Its main job is not cleaning water, but it can hold back some pollutants and sediment. Sand filters work on the same principle. They suit runoff from car parks and dense built-up areas.

nature-nbs-186.title: Sedimentation basins: the first stop for dirty runoff
nature-nbs-186.text: A sedimentation basin holds stormwater briefly and slows it, so that coarse and medium sediments settle to the bottom. It is often the first element in a treatment train, a series of steps that clean water in turn. By catching sediment early, it keeps later elements from being smothered. Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

nature-nbs-172.title: Retention basins: ponds that never dry
nature-nbs-172.text: A retention basin, also called a wet pond, is an artificial pond with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water. It manages stormwater by controlling runoff, guarding against floods and erosion, and improving the quality of nearby water. It differs from a detention basin, or 'dry pond', which holds water only after a storm and then drains at a controlled rate. It also differs from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

nature-nbs-204.title: Four families of permeable pavement
nature-nbs-204.text: Permeable pavement comes in several families, each suited to different uses. Pervious concrete is widely available and carries frequent traffic. Porous asphalt is laid like normal asphalt but leaves out the fine aggregate, so open voids let water through. Plastic grids filled with gravel or turf make a fully porous surface popular with homeowners. Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have open spaces between units and carry both light and heavy traffic.

nature-nbs-207.title: Room for the River: the Dutch stop raising dikes
nature-nbs-207.text: In 1993 and 1995, floods forced the evacuation of over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta. The Dutch response was Room for the River, a government plan run from 2006 to 2015. It protects against floods by giving rivers more space while improving landscape and environment. Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains and the low cross-walls that trap sand, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass. A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion. Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with the river's natural dynamics.

nature-nbs-202.title: The flood pulse concept: why floods feed rivers
nature-nbs-202.text: Older theories saw floods as catastrophes. The flood pulse concept, developed by W. J. Junk in 1989, sees the annual flood as the most biologically productive feature of a river ecosystem. The regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between channel and floodplain. The pulse maintains species and genetic diversity and brings in oxygen. Dams, channelization and levees disrupt it and can devastate riverside ecosystems. It is one of three main models of large rivers. Many theorists criticize its assumptions and prefer the river continuum concept, while its authors argue that rival does not fit large rivers.

nature-nbs-196.title: Beaver dam analogs: building dams for beavers
nature-nbs-196.text: People can build a beaver's dam for it. A beaver dam analog is a human-made structure that imitates a beaver dam, either to gain its benefits or to coax beavers into settling. Builders may drive wooden posts into the stream bed to hold branches that would otherwise wash away. Even if beavers never move in, analogs provide many of the benefits of natural dams, such as holding water and creating wetland ponds.

nature-nbs-201.title: Taming a dam without tearing it down
nature-nbs-201.text: Fewer than 1% of US dams are being considered for removal, so most rivers need other fixes. Better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders can reduce a dam's harm while it stays. Varying the water released by season mimics a river's natural flow changes. How well fish ladders help fish reach spawning grounds is debated, though some fish passing beats none. Plans for decommissioning and river restoration should be drawn up well before a dam reaches the end of its design life.

nature-nbs-200.title: Four ways to take down a dam
nature-nbs-200.text: Removing a dam is mostly a question of what to do with the sediment behind it. There are four common methods. Notch and release drains the reservoir slowly through cut notches, so the ecosystem can adjust; it can take over a year. Rapid release is quickest and cheapest but can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream. Dig and dewater, usually the most expensive, removes dried sediment for safe disposal, which is needed when it contains toxins. Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

nature-nbs-206.title: Replanting riverbanks: plant them or let them return
nature-nbs-206.text: Riverside plants can come back in two ways. Active revegetation plants them. Passive revegetation removes the disturbance and lets them return on their own. Active planting may be fastest but can cost too much. Passive methods can work well: fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities. The risk is that exotic species colonize first and undermine the recovery.

nature-nbs-193.title: Engineered log jams: putting wood back in rivers
nature-nbs-193.text: Straightened channels and the loss of beavers stripped many streams of their natural log jams. An engineered log jam places large wood back in a stream to recreate them. The logs change how water moves. They add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow, giving the stream more varied places for life.

nature-nbs-189.title: Form-based restoration: reshaping the channel
nature-nbs-189.text: Form-based stream restoration changes a channel's physical shape to improve its condition. Its tools include deflectors, cross-vanes, weirs and step-pools, engineered log jams, bank stabilization and redesigning the channel. The change is immediate. But it can fail when the damage comes from a wider area than the reach being fixed. Scientists criticize the approach on two counts. They say it works at too small a scale, and that it aims for what people think a stream should look like rather than what its setting supports.

nature-nbs-191.title: Natural Channel Design: a cookbook for streams
nature-nbs-191.text: Natural Channel Design is a US method from the 1990s. It classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed, then redesigns the channel to a target form. The design phase alone has 8 phases and 40 steps. Fluvial geomorphologists, who study how rivers shape land, are critical. They call it a 'cookbook' approach that untrained practitioners misuse, leading to failed projects. Its focus on channel stability can also limit a stream's ability to adapt.

nature-nbs-190.title: Process-based restoration: let the river do the work
nature-nbs-190.text: Process-based stream restoration rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form. It has grown in popularity since the mid-1990s as a more ecosystem-centred approach. It restores connections between stream and floodplain and along the stream itself, often by removing levees, dams or grade controls. The aim is a system that is as resilient as possible and needs little maintenance. The catch is patience, because benefits can take time to appear.

nature-nbs-192.title: Freedom space: a corridor for a wandering river
nature-nbs-192.text: Rivers move, and some planners now let them. A stream corridor, or freedom space, is a band of land set by a stream's hydrology and landforms within which it may move with minimal interference. The idea has many names. It is the river corridor in the US, room for the river in the Netherlands, and making space for water in the UK. A cost-benefit analysis found it could pay off over the long term through lower maintenance costs, less erosion and flood damage, and ecological services.

nature-nbs-194.title: Streambank bioengineering: roots instead of rock
nature-nbs-194.text: Stream banks can be held in place by living plants. Streambank bioengineering stabilizes banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap, loose rock armor, and gabions, wire cages of stone. Live branches sprout roots that anchor the soil and prevent erosion. That makes these structures more natural and adaptable than concrete and rock. Some bank erosion is welcome anyway, since it is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riverside habitats.

nature-nbs-175.title: The first flush: a storm's dirtiest minutes
nature-nbs-175.text: The first runoff of a rainstorm is the dirtiest. This first flush washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces, and in towns and suburbs it is described as highly toxic. Bioswales are built to handle it, which is why they suit roads, parking lots and roofs. Rainwater tanks may use a first-flush diverter to keep contaminants out of the stored water.

nature-nbs-208.title: Source water protection: guarding drinking water at the start
nature-nbs-208.text: In Walkerton, Ontario, drinking water was contaminated with E. coli. Canada responded by adopting source water protection as part of a multi-barrier approach. Source water protection is planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination. It applies to lakes, rivers and groundwater. The work involves identifying sources, assessing contamination threats, informing the public and acting to remove contamination. Researchers have begun bringing ecosystem service assessments into source water protection.

reviews.water-and-flood-solutions: Cities turn rain into a hazard, because hard surfaces stop it soaking in and drains rush it toward rivers, carrying pollution and flooding streets. The old answer was grey infrastructure: pipes, walls and reservoirs that fight water and grow less effective as floods intensify. The newer answer copies nature, with rain gardens, bioswales, permeable paving, constructed wetlands, sponge cities and rivers given room to spread, as at Nijmegen and across the Netherlands. The money often favors green, as Philadelphia's plan showed, though new parks can price out poorer residents. Restored floodplains handle frequent floods well, while the extreme ones still call for barriers and walls, so the best results come from mixing the two.
